description: We are a fully formed team of 4 specializing in AI, ERP, and Audio Engineering. Our tech stack includes Python, OpenCV, YOLO, FastAPI, and local LLMs. We are focusing on the Martian Map challenge. Please note: Our team is complete and we are not accepting new members.
summary:
Martian Map is a mission-rehearsal simulator that lets an astronaut walk a Mars EVA before it happens and see the true cost of every route choice.

  We built it on real NASA data from Gale Crater's boxwork region, where Curiosity is driving today:
  - Terrain: HiRISE 1 m elevation and 25 cm orthophoto.
  - Ground photos: 391 Curiosity Navcam frames from 128 stops.
  - Radiation: dose rate measured by Curiosity's RAD instrument.

  A DeepLabv3+ model trained on AI4Mars labels sand, soil, bedrock and big rocks in those photos and reports where it is unsure. A planner searches a 2 m grid with
  Dijkstra and offers three routes: shortest, balanced and safest. It turns slope, rocks and terrain type into time, energy, oxygen and dose using the Pandolf equation
  calibrated to Apollo EVA data, and it closes slopes above 20°, following NASA's EVA guideline. In 3D, the astronaut walks the route, scans hazards, compares real Navcam
  photos with the simulation, and gets replanned around sand.

  This matters because the route sets how much of the life-support budget a walk consumes. Martian Map shows that cost before anyone steps outside. It is an independent
  prototype: we checked it against Curiosity's real traverse and state its limits, notably weak sand detection.
details:
What it does. Martian Map lets an astronaut rehearse a Mars spacewalk before it happens.

- Briefing and route choice: After reading a mission briefing, the astronaut picks one of three routes (shortest, balanced, safest), each priced in minutes, kcal,

litres of O₂ and µGy of radiation.

- 3D rehearsal: The astronaut walks the chosen route on real HiRISE terrain of Gale Crater, where Curiosity is driving today.

- Oxygen, energy, time and dose update with every step.

- A return-margin gauge and a GO / NO-GO badge show when to turn back.

- A scanner marks caution and no-go ground.

- A helmet camera opens Curiosity's real Navcam photo at that spot, with our model's terrain prediction overlaid.

- When a sand patch appears, the route line redraws around it.

- Sample, return and debrief: At the target the astronaut collects a sample, and the return is re-planned with the heavier load. A debrief compares plan with outcome.

- Own routes: Users can also plan their own route between any two points.

How it works.

1. Data layers.

- Slope from the USGS HiRISE DTM (1 m).

- Rock cover from our shadow-based detector on the HiRISE orthophoto (25 cm).

- Terrain-class probabilities (soil, bedrock, sand, big rock) with an uncertainty value, from a DeepLabv3+ (ResNet34) model trained on AI4Mars and applied to 391

Curiosity Navcam frames at 128 stops.

2. Cost model.

- The Pandolf walking-energy equation with Soule-Goldman terrain factors, scaled to Mars gravity and calibrated to the Apollo EVA average of 272 W (NASA SP-368).

- Slopes of 20° and above are closed (NASA EVA Lunar Surface ConOps, EVA-EXP-0075); 15° is flagged as caution.

- Budgets are sourced: 7 h and 1,800 kcal (Apollo 15–17 PLSS, SP-368); 375 L O₂ derived from that energy budget; body, suit and load masses from NASA-STD-3001 and

NASA JSC (Ogilvie et al. 2026).

3. Planner (FastAPI).

- A Dijkstra least-cost search on a 2 m grid (1,000 × 1,000 cells, 8-neighbour, no corner cutting).

- Each cell's cost is a weighted sum of time, energy and risk. The three routes are three weightings of the same search.

- Endpoints: /replan for observations, /compare (slope-only vs. terrain model), and /assumptions, which lists every parameter with its source.

4. Simulator (Three.js).

- Streamed terrain tiles and a live route, re-planned from the current position about every 3 m.

- Navcam viewing direction from the NASA CAHVOR camera model.

- An optional in-browser ONNX run of the terrain model.

Benefits and intended impact. A pre-EVA briefing tool for astronauts and mission planners. They see what a route costs before anyone goes outside, compare options, and

know which numbers are measurements, which are model estimates and which are assumptions. Near-term use: analog missions and crew training.

Creativity. We put the astronaut inside the data instead of drawing a line on a map. Curiosity's own photos act as a check inside the simulator: a slider moves between

the real Navcam photo and our simulated view at the same spot, so anyone can judge how well it matches. The model also shows where it is unsure, not only what it

predicts.

Factors we considered.

- Site choice: verifiability. We chose Gale because every claim can be checked there.

- The terrain model's training labels come largely from Curiosity.

- Radiation was measured on site by Curiosity's RAD.

- Curiosity's real traverse serves as ground truth.

- Honesty about limits.

- Energy coefficients are Earth measurements, and slope limits come from lunar planning, not Mars-validated human data.

- Rocks and ground texture in the 3D view are synthetic and labelled as such.

- Validation.

- Terrain model on the expert-labelled AI4Mars test set: mIoU 0.798, large-rock recall 0.973, pixel calibration error (ECE) 0.004.

- Dominant terrain correct at 16 of 18 hand-checked Navcam stops.

- Routes run about 130 m from Curiosity's real track (geometry only).

- The scanner matched 3 of 6 stops; both misses were sandy. Sand is our weakest point, and the app says so.

Tools.

- Python, FastAPI, NumPy, SciPy, scikit-image, rasterio/GDAL.

- PyTorch (DeepLabv3+, U-Net), ONNX Runtime Web.

- Three.js, React + Leaflet.

- Playwright, pytest and node:test.

Hardware. We trained the model on a consumer NVIDIA GPU. The simulator runs in a standard web browser with no installation.
